summary:
Buenos Aires province stands under Argentina's national framework for gender recognition and implements that regime through its own civil registry. The provincial ombudsman published a guide in September 2024 setting out the steps for rectifying the gender marker of people born in the province, including provisions for people born in Buenos Aires province who now live elsewhere.

The provincial ombudsman's Gender Violence Office, created by Resolución Nº 100/10, submitted evidence to the UN Human Rights Committee for its June and July 2016 review documenting violence, persecution and harassment of trans and travesti people in Buenos Aires province by provincial police and by third parties acting under police cover. The submission carries a dedicated section on violence by judicial, state and police agents.

Academic and legal research records the criminalisation of trans and travesti women in the province through drug-offence prosecutions brought under microtrafficking enforcement, concentrated in La Plata's Zona Roja. After the 2012 Gender Identity Law formally decriminalised trans presence, security-led street-offence policing became the operative instrument of indirect criminalisation in the province.

That instrument rests on a jurisdictional transfer: in 2005 Buenos Aires province assumed jurisdiction over drug sale and possession offences, the devolution that allowed provincial street-offence and drug-law prosecution to function as the enforcement route.

No trans-specific placement rule for prisoners is recorded for the province. Buenos Aires province operates no separate trans housing unit and no province-level rule on where trans women are held; placement is governed by the national prison-housing framework.
tangentialFactors:
The documented exposure of trans and travesti women in Buenos Aires province runs through policing and prosecution rather than through the recognition statute, which is unchanged at the national level.

The provincial ombudsman's office is the main provincial institution producing trans-specific documentation, through its Gender Violence Office and its registry guide; its 2016 submission to the UN Human Rights Committee remains the provincial documentation of police violence against trans and travesti people.

The registry guide is diaspora-facing as well as local: it includes provisions for people born in Buenos Aires province who now live elsewhere.
localsOnly:
People born in Buenos Aires province can rectify their registered gender, image and birth name through the provincial civil registry; the ombudsman's September 2024 guide sets out the steps and covers applicants born in the province who live elsewhere.

The provincial ombudsman's Gender Violence Office, established by Resolución Nº 100/10, receives and documents complaints, and its 2016 submission to the UN Human Rights Committee records violence, persecution and harassment by provincial police and by third parties acting under police cover against trans and travesti people in the province.

Trans and travesti women in the province face drug-offence prosecution under microtrafficking enforcement, documented in La Plata's Zona Roja; provincial jurisdiction over drug sale and possession offences dates from 2005.

No province-level rule governs the placement of trans women in provincial prisons, and no separate trans housing unit is recorded.
outOfScopeNotes:
No provincial statistics disaggregating prosecutions, convictions or violence by gender identity are available; the documented pattern rests on a 2016 ombudsman submission to the UN Human Rights Committee and on academic and legal-analysis research.

No count of drug-offence prosecutions of trans and travesti women in Buenos Aires province is available, nor years or outcomes; the concentration in La Plata's Zona Roja is documented without figures.

The absence of a province-level prison placement rule is recorded through a source focused on the national prison policy; no provincial instrument on trans prisoners is cited.

Whether the provincial police practices documented in 2016 continue at the same level is unresolved; no post-2016 provincial documentation of police violence against trans and travesti people is available.
